# What the simulation says about the parameters

*Generated by `node lab/search-v2/tools/simulate.mjs`. 30 simulated participants (15 on sequence A, 15 on B), each playing all 28 rounds of the real frozen artifacts — the same pool, the same 28 specs, the same AI — under seven policies, with a counterfactual re-play of every AI-ON round. Every number below comes from that run. Nothing is asserted that the simulator did not measure.*

## 1 · The costs (reveal 5, question 2)

The 5:2 ratio works: the AI is worth consulting, which is the premise of the study.
RATIONAL-WITH-AI scores 68.76 where the same searcher without an AI scores 63.93, spending 13.5 points a round against 9.5.

The LEVEL, however, is the design's weakest parameter, and the number that shows it is
the floor. A participant who spends nothing and nominates what the interface already
offers scores 58.17. Myopic unaided search — §16.8's own benchmark — scores 63.93,
i.e. it buys +5.76 points for 9.5 points of effort. Systematic unaided search,
which opens the line until no gap is wider than g* = 18.8, scores 44.71 — -13.46 against
doing nothing, because 8.9 reveals cost 44.4 and the prize surface has a mean of 62.

So in the AI-OFF arm there is almost nothing for effort to buy, and the myopic
benchmark stops after 1.89 reveals a round. That is not a bug in the benchmark: at
c_R = 5 it is the correct myopic answer. It does mean the AI-OFF arm is close to a
no-search arm, which narrows every contrast the study is trying to draw.

| | mean score | questions | reveals | spent | net of the do-nothing floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| spend nothing (floor) | 58.17 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.0 | +0.00 |
| myopic search, no AI | 63.93 | 0.00 | 1.89 | 9.5 | +5.76 |
| systematic search, no AI | 44.71 | 0.00 | 8.88 | 44.4 | -13.46 |
| rational, with AI | 68.76 | 4.86 | 0.76 | 13.5 | +10.59 |
| trusting, with AI | 70.07 | 4.16 | 0.44 | 10.5 | +11.90 |

## 2 · K = 4 and K = 10 — the straddle holds, the sign flip does not follow

The geometry is exactly as designed. Measured over every position of every scored spec,
with the AI's anchor set as the round begins:

`  sparse   mean sd 10.87   41.4% of the line above s* = 12.53   mean |AI error| 8.56`
`  dense    mean sd 7.08   1.0% of the line above s*             mean |AI error| 5.76`

The two densities are separated by a factor of 1.5 in how wrong the AI is, and the
verification threshold lands between them. The design's premise is sound.

What does NOT follow is a sign change in SCORE. Per-participant crossover effects:

| policy | sparse effect | dense effect | sparse − dense | n@80% for the interaction | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RATIONAL-WITH-AI | +2.75 | +7.07 | -4.32 | 60 | gradient |
| TRUSTING | +3.71 | +8.31 | -4.61 | 39 | gradient |
| SKEPTICAL | +1.36 | -1.36 | +2.72 | 217 | **flip** |
| NOISY-SATISFICER | +0.52 | +2.69 | -2.18 | 244 | gradient |

A sign flip is present for SKEPTICAL. For the others the contrast is a
GRADIENT: the AI is worth less in sparse rounds than in dense ones, by up to 4.61 points,
but it does not cross zero. Report the interaction, not "the AI hurts in sparse rounds".


The window in which a flip could exist at all is narrow and it is a property of the
REVEAL COST, not of K: s* = c_R·√(2π) has to fall between the two nominal mid-gap
standard deviations, 9.13 (dense) and 14.43 (sparse), so

`c_R must lie in (3.64, 5.76)  —  and it is 5, almost exactly mid-window.`

Equivalently, at c_R = 5 the K that sits exactly on the threshold is K* = 5.31:
sparse must be below it and dense above it, and K = 4 / K = 10 straddle it with 15%
and 27% of margin. Nothing about the two K values needs to move.

## 3 · The caps (40 questions, 20 reveals)

Neither cap binds, on any policy. The heaviest questioner is RATIONAL-WITH-AI at 4.86 questions
a round against a cap of 40; the heaviest revealer is SYSTEMATIC-NO-AI at 8.88 of 20.
The highest share of rounds touching either cap is 0.0% (NOISY-SATISFICER).
The caps are doing their intended job — bounding a pathological session — and nothing
else. Leave them. They are not what limits search here; the reveal cost is.

## 4 · 24 scored rounds

Twelve rounds a condition is enough for every effect a plausible participant produces:

| contrast | effect (points) | paired sd | participants for 80% power |
|---|---|---|---|
| RATIONAL-WITH-AI (score) | +4.91 | 2.67 | 3 |
| TRUSTING (score) | +6.01 | 3.58 | 3 |
| SKEPTICAL (score) | -0.00 | 4.02 | 16418414 |
| NOISY-SATISFICER (score) | +1.61 | 9.80 | 293 |
| RATIONAL-WITH-AI (frontier share) | -6.25pp | 6.36 | 9 |
| TRUSTING (frontier share) | -6.25pp | 6.36 | 9 |


The null policy — RATIONAL-NO-AI, which cannot see the condition at all — returns -0.05 with a
paired sd of 3.71. That is the simulator's own zero and the floor any real effect
has to clear; it also shows the two blocks are balanced, since a block difference would
appear here first.

The sparse-vs-dense INTERACTION is the expensive one: 39 participants for TRUSTING and 60
for RATIONAL-WITH-AI. If the interaction is the headline, 24 scored rounds is the
parameter to move, not the sample: the paired sd falls with the square root of the
rounds per cell, so 16 scored rounds per condition would cut the required n by about a
third at the same recruitment cost per participant.

## 5 · The three layouts

| layout | frontier share of first moves — no AI | rational + AI | trusting | satisficer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRONTIER | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 91.7% |
| BALANCED | 42.9% | 37.5% | 37.5% | 9.3% |
| GAP | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 1.8% |


The three geometries separate the primary outcome cleanly and by a wide margin, with no
AI involved at all: a rational searcher goes to the frontier from FRONTIER and into the
gap from GAP, and BALANCED sits between them. That separation is the manipulation
working. Keep all three; they are the sharpest instrument in the design.

## 6 · What to move, and in which direction

The costs are adequate: unaided search buys +5.76 points over doing nothing, which is
enough for the AI-OFF arm to be a real search arm. No change recommended.

**Leave alone:** the two K values (they straddle K* = 5.31 with 15% and 27% of margin,
and the measured AI error differs between them by a factor of 1.5); the caps (neither binds,
on any policy); the three layouts (they separate the primary outcome by 100 points of
frontier share with no AI in the picture); and the question cost of 2, which is what makes
the AI worth consulting in the first place.

**Expect a gradient, not a flip.** A sign change does appear for SKEPTICAL, but not for every policy, so
a pre-registration that predicts "the AI helps at K = 10 and hurts at K = 4" is
predicting something this environment does not reliably produce. Predict the
INTERACTION instead — the AI is worth less when it is sparse — and power for it: 39
participants at 24 scored rounds, against 3 for the main effect.

## Appendix · the seven policies

| policy | what it does | AI-OFF behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| BLIND-GUESS | spends nothing, nominates the best pre-opened position (or mid-line) | same |
| RATIONAL-NO-AI | myopic expected improvement on its own reveals; stops when the best EI < c_R | same |
| SYSTEMATIC-NO-AI | reveals the widest stretch until no gap exceeds g* and no tail exceeds (s*/σ)² | same |
| RATIONAL-WITH-AI | probes by asking, verifies a new front-runner only where its own uncertainty exceeds s* | RATIONAL-NO-AI |
| TRUSTING | treats an answer as a fact, converges on the AI's curve, verifies 10% of the time | RATIONAL-NO-AI |
| SKEPTICAL | asks 0–4 questions, ignores every answer, searches as RATIONAL-NO-AI | RATIONAL-NO-AI |
| NOISY-SATISFICER | probes the widest gap, stops on anything above a personal threshold, 10% random actions; an AI answer counts as something held | itself, revealing instead of asking |
